advice.title: Antenatal danger signs
advice.text: Come to hospital at once if you have bleeding from the vagina, leaking of water, severe headache or blurred vision, fits, swelling of the face or hands, severe abdominal pain, fever, difficulty breathing, or if the baby moves less than usual.

advice.title: Diet and supplements in pregnancy
advice.text: Eat an extra meal each day with pulses, green leafy vegetables, fruit and milk. Take the iron-folic acid and calcium tablets exactly as prescribed, not at the same time. Do not use tobacco or alcohol.

advice.title: Danger signs after delivery
advice.text: Come back at once for heavy bleeding, fever, foul-smelling discharge, severe headache, fits, breathlessness, pain or swelling in one leg, or a painful red breast.

advice.title: Fever: care at home and when to come back
advice.text: Give plenty of fluids and keep feeding or breastfeeding. Give fever medicine only as prescribed for the child's weight. Come back at once if the child cannot drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, has a fit, becomes very sleepy or hard to wake, breathes fast or with difficulty, or has a rash that does not fade when pressed.

advice.title: Diarrhoea: ORS, zinc and when to come back
advice.text: Give ORS after every loose stool and keep feeding or breastfeeding. Give the zinc tablets every day for as many days as prescribed, even after the diarrhoea stops. Come back at once if the child drinks poorly, becomes sicker, has blood in the stool, or passes very little urine.

advice.title: Breastfeeding and complementary feeding
advice.text: Give only breast milk, no water or other milk, for the first 6 months. From 6 months add soft family foods, 2 to 3 meals a day at 6 to 8 months and 3 to 4 meals a day from 9 months with 1 to 2 snacks, and keep breastfeeding to 2 years or beyond. During illness give more fluids and more frequent breastfeeds.

advice.title: Newborn danger signs
advice.text: Bring the baby at once if the baby is not feeding well, has a fit, breathes fast or with difficulty, feels hot or cold, moves less than usual, has yellow palms or soles, or has redness or pus around the cord.

advice.title: Caring for your plaster
advice.text: Keep the limb raised, especially for the first few days, and do not let it hang down. Move the fingers or toes and the joints outside the plaster often. Keep the plaster dry and away from fire, and contact the hospital if it cracks, becomes soft, loose or tight, or anything falls inside it.

advice.title: Plaster warning signs
advice.text: Come back at once if the pain keeps getting worse, the fingers or toes become blue, swollen, numb or tingling or you cannot move them, you get pain in the calf, chest pain or breathlessness, or there is rubbing, discharge, wetness or a bad smell under the plaster.

advice.title: Back pain or sciatica: when to come at once
advice.text: Come to hospital at once if you get numbness between your legs or around your back passage or genitals, difficulty passing or controlling urine, leaking urine or stools, loss of feeling when you pass urine or stools, new weakness in both legs, or a change in sexual function.

advice.title: When to come back at once
advice.text: Come back the same day if your sight gets worse, the eye becomes more painful or red, light starts to hurt your eyes, or you notice new floaters, flashes of light or a shadow spreading across your vision. Any sudden loss of sight needs to be seen the same day, even if it recovers.

advice.title: Red eye: stopping the spread
advice.text: Wash your hands often, use your own towel and pillow, and avoid close contact with others for 10 to 14 days while the eye is red and watery. Do not put steroid drops, leftover drops or home remedies in the eye unless your eye doctor has advised them.

advice.title: Diabetes and your eyes
advice.text: If you have diabetes, have a dilated eye examination at least once a year, even when you see well, because early damage gives no symptoms and early treatment works best. Keeping blood sugar and blood pressure under control lowers the risk of losing sight.

advice.title: Protecting your eyes
advice.text: Wear protective glasses for farm work, grinding, welding and sport, and keep children away from firecrackers. Stopping smoking lowers the risk of cataract and macular disease. Have eye problems checked by a trained eye doctor rather than using remedies from untrained providers.

advice.title: Caring for your ears
advice.text: Do not put cotton buds, hairpins, oil or home remedies into the ears; wax usually comes out by itself. Keep dirty water out of the ears when bathing or swimming. See a doctor soon for ear pain, discharge, bleeding or hearing loss, and on the same day if hearing is lost suddenly.

advice.title: Protecting your hearing
advice.text: Keep phone and earphone volume below 60% of maximum, limit listening time and take breaks from loud sound. Use ear plugs or ear muffs in noisy work and at loud events, and keep away from loudspeakers.

advice.title: Nosebleed first aid
advice.text: If your nose bleeds, stay calm, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for at least 5 minutes; if it slows, keep holding for a full 15 minutes. Avoid picking the nose or blowing it hard, and keep the inside moist with saline spray or gel. Do not stop a blood thinner without asking the doctor who prescribed it. Go to the emergency department if bleeding is heavy or will not stop, or if you feel weak or faint.

advice.title: Tobacco and warning signs
advice.text: Stop all forms of tobacco, including cigarettes, bidis, gutkha, khaini and tobacco paan, stop chewing areca nut (supari), and cut down alcohol. See a doctor if a mouth ulcer has not healed in 3 weeks, or if you notice a red or white patch in the mouth, a lump in the neck, or a hoarse voice that does not go away.

advice.title: Serious drug reaction: warning signs
advice.text: Come to hospital at once if you get fever with a sore throat or sore red eyes, a painful red or purple rash, blisters or peeling skin, or sores in the mouth, eyes or genitals. If a medicine caused your skin reaction, keep a record of its name, tell every doctor and pharmacist, and do not start any new medicine, even one bought without a prescription, before asking your doctor.

advice.title: Leprosy: treatment and self-care
advice.text: Leprosy is curable. Take the multidrug treatment regularly until the full course is finished. If your hands or feet are numb, check them every day for cuts, burns, blisters or red spots, soak dry skin in water and then apply oil or moisturiser, and wear footwear with a soft inner sole. Come back at once if patches become red and swollen, or you get nerve pain, new numbness or weakness, painful lumps with fever, or red eyes.

advice.title: Fungal skin infection (ringworm)
advice.text: Use the antifungal medicine regularly and continue it as advised, usually for 2 weeks after the rash clears. Do not apply steroid or mixed creams bought without a prescription. Wear loose clothes and change them when sweaty, do not share towels, bed linen or clothes, wash undergarments and socks often and dry them in the sun, and get family members with a similar rash examined.

advice.title: Scabies: treat everyone together
advice.text: Everyone in the household and other close contacts must be treated at the same time, even if they do not itch. Wash clothes, towels and bed linen when you start treatment, and seal anything that cannot be washed in a bag for 3 days. Itching often carries on for a few weeks after the mites are killed.

advice.title: Help in a crisis
advice.text: If you have thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, tell someone you trust and get help straight away: go to the nearest hospital emergency department, or call Tele MANAS on 14416 or 1800-89-14416 (free, 24 hours a day). Keep your safety plan and these numbers with you.

advice.title: Keeping the home safe
advice.text: Ask a family member to lock away all medicines, pesticides, acids and other poisons, and to remove anything else you might use to harm yourself. Share your safety plan with them so they know your warning signs and whom to call.

advice.title: Taking antidepressants
advice.text: Antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start working and up to 6 weeks for the full effect, so take them every day even if you notice no change at first. Do not stop them suddenly, and do not take extra to make up for a missed dose. Carry on for as long as your doctor advises, usually at least six months after you feel better. Tell your doctor straight away about troublesome side effects or any thoughts of harming yourself, and ask before drinking alcohol or driving.

advice.title: Daily care of teeth and gums
advice.text: Brush your teeth twice a day for at least two minutes with a fluoride toothpaste. Cut down sweets, sugary snacks and fizzy drinks, especially between meals, and drink water instead. Have your mouth checked by a dentist regularly.

advice.title: Tobacco, areca nut and mouth cancer
advice.text: Stop all tobacco, smoked or chewed (bidi, cigarettes, gutka, khaini), and areca nut (supari, paan). Tobacco damages the gums, and tobacco and areca nut are leading causes of mouth cancer; ask us for help to quit. Look inside your mouth regularly, and see a dentist or doctor without delay if an ulcer or a white or red patch has not healed in 2 weeks. Do not put tobacco or anything else on it.

advice.title: Toothache and swelling
advice.text: Until your treatment, keep the area clean and rinse with warm salt water. Do not put tobacco, camphor, salt, balm or heat on the tooth or the swollen cheek, and take only the medicines prescribed for you. Go to the hospital emergency department at once if the swelling spreads, or you have fever or difficulty opening your mouth, swallowing or breathing.

advice.title: After a tooth extraction
advice.text: If the socket bleeds, place a rolled, damp gauze or clean cotton pad over it and bite firmly for 20 minutes. For the next 24 hours avoid smoking, alcohol and exercise, keep your head raised and do not disturb the clot. If bleeding continues after a second 20 minutes of pressure, come to the hospital straight away; if you take blood-thinning medicine, come as soon as bleeding fails to stop or starts again.

actEarly: Developmental milestones are things most children (75% or more) can do by a certain age.
You know your child best. Don't wait. If your child is not meeting one or more milestones, has lost skills he or she once had, or you have other concerns, act early.
Talk with your child's doctor, share your concerns, and ask about developmental screening.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that children be screened for general development using standardized, validated tools at 9, 18, and 30 months and for autism at 18 and 24 months or whenever a parent or provider has a concern.
If you or the doctor are still concerned, ask for a referral to a specialist who can evaluate your child more.
If you or the doctor are still concerned, call your state or territory's early intervention program to find out if your child can get services to help.
Learn the Signs. Act Early. materials are not a substitute for standardized, validated developmental screening tools.
